Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 1:

﴿Fear your Lord⦆ We have spoken about taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) at the beginning of al-Baqarah. ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour⦆ means its severity and its terror, as in His saying: ﴿and they were shaken⦆ [al-Baqarah 2:214; al-Ahzab 33:11], or the shaking of the earth at that time, as in His saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake⦆ [al-Zalzalah 99:1]. The clause is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to taqwa. Scholars differed over whether the convulsion and the hardships mentioned after it occur in this world before the Resurrection, or after the Resurrection has taken place. The more preponderant view is that it is before the Resurrection, because at that time there will be the distraction of the nursing mother and the laying down of the pregnant woman's burden, not after the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 2:

﴿On the Day you see it﴾ The governing element of the time phrase is "will be distracted" (tadhhalu). The pronoun refers to the quake (al-zalzala). It has also been said that it refers to the Hour (al-sa'a), but this is weak for the reason we have mentioned, unless he means the beginning of its matter. ﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted﴾ Dhuhul (distraction) is departing from a thing together with bewilderment. ﴿Nursing mother (murdi'a)﴾ He did not say "murdi'" (a nursing mother by nature), because the murdi'a is the one who, in the state of nursing, is putting her breast to the child's mouth, whereas the mur-di' is one whose nature is to nurse even if she is not actually nursing at the time being described. So he said "murdi'a" so that this would be more intense in its distraction, since she would then be pulling her breast away from the child's mouth. ﴿And you will see people as drunk﴾ This is a comparison to drunkards because of the severity of grief. ﴿But they are not drunk﴾ This negates the reality of intoxication. He (another reader) read "sakra" (sukra), and the meaning is the same.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And among mankind is one who disputes about Allah﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it is said concerning Abu Jahl. It encompasses everyone who is characterized by this trait. ﴿Following every rebellious devil﴾ That is, one who is intensely misleading. It is possible that he intends a devil of the jinn or of mankind.

Kutiba (﴿كُتِبَ﴾): a metaphor for the matter being established, as if it were written down. It may also mean "decreed" (qada), as in your saying "God has written (kataba Allah) that..." In that case it is in the position of the object whose agent is not named. "Anna" (that) is governed by it, and "wa-fi annahu" is a conjunction linked to it. It has also been said that it is an emphatic repetition.

﴿مَن تَوَلاَّهُ﴾ means: whoever follows him (tabi'ahu) or takes him as a patron (wali). The pronoun in "alayhi" and in "annahu" in both places, and in "tawallahu," refers to the Satan. The pronoun in "yudilluhu" and "yahdihi" refers to the one who takes him as a patron. It is also possible that those pronouns originally refer to the one who disputes.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 5:

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ etc.: its meaning is: if you doubt the otherworldly resurrection, then the removal of that doubt is that you look at the beginning of your creation; you will then know that He who was able to create you the first time is able to restore you a second time, and that He who was able to bring plants out of the earth after its death is able to bring you out of your graves. ﴿We created you from dust﴾ refers to the creation of Adam, and it is attributed to people because they are his descendants and he is their origin. ﴿From a clinging clot﴾: the 'alaqah is a piece of congealed blood. ﴿From a lump of flesh﴾: i.e., a piece of flesh. ﴿Formed and unformed﴾: the mukhallaqah is the one whose creation is complete, and the ghayr mukhallaqah is the incomplete one, such as a miscarriage. It was also said: the mukhallaqah is the one that is shaped and sound, free of deficiency. ﴿That We may make clear to you﴾: the lam is connected to an omitted element whose estimated meaning is: We mentioned that. ﴿That We may make clear to you﴾: Our power over resurrection. ﴿And We settle﴾: a new verb (fi'l mustanaf). ﴿In a term appointed﴾: meaning the time of delivering the womb, which varies; its minimum is six months and it may be more than that. ﴿Then We bring you forth as infants﴾: he used the singular because he intended the genus, or he intended that We bring forth each one of you as an infant. ﴿That you may reach your maturity﴾: this is the full completion of strength, intellect and discernment. It has been differed upon, from eighteen years to forty-five. ﴿The most abject term of life﴾: mentioned in al-Nahl [16:70]. ﴿Dead﴾: meaning there is no plant in it. ﴿It stirs﴾: it moves with plant growth, and its parts loosen when water enters it. ﴿And swells﴾: it swells up. ﴿Of every lovely kind﴾: i.e., a wondrous variety.

﴿ذٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾ That refers to what was mentioned concerning the matter of man and plants, which is established, because God is the Truth. This is how al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) understood it, and the bāʾ (preposition) on this reading is causal (sababiyya). Ibn ʿAṭiyya (d. 541 AH) also explained it in this sense. It follows from this that ﴿وَأَنَّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ﴾ ("and that the Hour is coming") cannot be coordinated with ﴿ذٰلِكَ﴾, because it is not a cause of what was mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said regarding ﴿وَأَنَّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ آتِيَةٌ﴾ that it is not a cause of what was mentioned, but the meaning is that the matter is interconnected, or that it is to be read with an implied "and the matter is that the Hour..." Both of these answers given by Ibn ʿAṭiyya are weak. As for his saying that the matter is interconnected, the connection here can only be through coordination (ʿaṭf), and coordination is not valid. As for his saying that it is to be read as an implied "the matter is that the Hour...", that is a resumption (istiʾnāf) that cuts off the first statement, and there is no doubt that the purpose of the first statement is to establish the Hour. How then can its mention be made separate from what precedes it?

What appears to me is that the bāʾ is not causal. Rather, a verb should be supplied for it that it attaches to and that the meaning requires. The supplied sense would be: "That which has preceded of the creation of man and plants is evidence that God is the Truth, that He gives life to the dead, and that the Hour is coming." On this reading, ﴿وَأَنَّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ﴾ can validly be coordinated with what precedes it, and these matters mentioned after ﴿ذٰلِكَ﴾ are those for which the creation of man and plants serves as proof.

And among the people is he who argues about Allah without knowledge. It was revealed concerning those about whom the first (verse) was revealed, and it is said: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

﴿Turning aside in arrogance﴾ is a metonymy (kināya) for the proud one who turns away. ﴿For him in this world there is disgrace﴾. If it was revealed about al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, then the disgrace was that he was taken captive and then killed. The same applies to the killing of Abu Jahl.

This is the tafsir of Ibn Juzayy in al-Tashil, on Surah al-Hajj, verse 10.

﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ — i.e., it is said to him: "That is because of what you did, and because of God's justice, for He does not wrong the servants."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verses 11–12:

﴿And among mankind is he who worships Allah on an edge (ḥarf). If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ It was revealed concerning a group of the Bedouin (al-aʿrab). One of them, when he embraced Islam and something pleasing happened to him in his wealth and children, would say: "This is a good religion." But if the opposite happened to him, he would consider it an ill omen and apostatize from Islam. So ḥarf here is a metaphor for purpose (maqṣid), and its root meaning is deviation from a thing, or it derives from ḥarf in the sense of "edge," meaning that he is at the fringe of the religion, not at its center. ﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter.﴾ The loss of this world is what befalls him in it, and the loss of the Hereafter is his apostasy and his corrupt belief. ﴿That which neither harms him nor benefits him.﴾ This refers to the idols. And ﴿yadʿū﴾ (calls upon) is used in the sense of ʿabada (worships) in both places.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verses 11–12:

﴿And among mankind is he who worships Allah on an edge (ḥarf). If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter.﴾ It was revealed concerning a group of the Bedouin (al-aʿrab). One of them, when he embraced Islam and something pleasing happened to him in his wealth and children, would say: "This is a good religion." But if the opposite happened to him, he would consider it an ill omen and apostatize from Islam. So ḥarf here is a metaphor for purpose (maqṣid), and its root meaning is deviation from a thing, or it derives from ḥarf in the sense of "edge," meaning that he is at the fringe of the religion, not at its center. ﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter.﴾ The loss of this world is what befalls him in it, and the loss of the Hereafter is his apostasy and his corrupt belief. ﴿That which neither harms him nor benefits him.﴾ This refers to the idols. And ﴿yadʿū﴾ (calls upon) is used in the sense of ʿabada (worships) in both places.

﴿يَدْعُو لَمَنْ ضَرُّهُ أَقْرَبُ مِن نَّفْعِهِ﴾ (He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit). In this verse there are two difficulties. The first concerns meaning: He describes the idols as neither harming nor benefiting, and then describes them as having harm nearer than benefit, so He negates harm and then affirms it. The answer is that the harm negated first refers to what proceeds from their own action, and they do nothing, while the second harm refers to what comes about through them, such as punishment and other things. The second difficulty concerns the particle اللام (lam, "for") entering on ﴿مِن﴾ (min, "whoever"), which in appearance is an object (maf'ul), and the lam does not enter on an object. People have answered this in three ways. The first is that the lam is moved forward from its proper place, as if the original were: "He calls upon whoever, for whose harm is nearer than his benefit," so its proper place is to enter upon the subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence). The second is that ﴿يَدْعُو﴾ (yad'u, "he calls upon") is repeated here for emphasis on the first ﴿يَدْعُو﴾, and the sentence is complete at that point; then he begins with ﴿لَمَنْ ضَرُّهُ﴾, so ﴿مِن﴾ is the subject and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿لَبِئْسَ ٱلْمَوْلَىٰ﴾ (surely wretched is the protector). The third is that the meaning of ﴿يَدْعُو﴾ is "he will say on the Day of Resurrection," which is a statement made when he sees the harm of the idols, so the lam entered upon a subject at the beginning of the sentence. ﴿ٱلْمَوْلَىٰ﴾ (al-mawla, "the protector") here means the ally (al-wali), and ﴿ٱلْعَشِيرُ﴾ (al-ashir, "the companion") means the associate, being from the same tribe (al-ashira).

Verse 14 of Surah al-Hajj: Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds [into gardens beneath which rivers flow].

Ibn Juzayy: When He mentioned that the idols do not benefit those who worship them, He contrasted this with the fact that Allah benefits those who worship Him with the greatest benefit, which is admission into Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 15:

﴿Then let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut off [his breath]﴾. The sabab (rope) here is the cord, and the sky here is the ceiling of the house and similar things from which cords are hung. The "cutting off" here is intended to mean strangling oneself with the rope; it is said: "qata'a al-rajul" when a man was strangled. It may also be intended to mean cutting oneself off from the ground after tying the rope around the neck and fastening it to the ceiling. By "strangulation" here is meant what is done by one whose rage and grief have become intense, or who covets what he cannot attain, like the saying to the envious person: "Die of rage, or strangle yourself; for you cannot do otherwise."

There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the verse. The first: the pronoun in "yansurahu" (He will help him) refers to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning according to this is: whoever among the disbelievers thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad, let him strangle himself with a rope, for Allah is his helper without doubt, in spite of the rage of the disbelievers. So what causes the strangulation is the rage at the support of our master Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second opinion: the pronoun in ﴿yansurahu﴾ refers back to ﴿man﴾ (whoever). The meaning according to this is: whoever, because of the constriction of his chest and the abundance of his distress, thinks that Allah will not help him, let him strangle himself and die of his rage, for he cannot do otherwise. So what causes the strangulation according to this is despair and discontent with the decree, and evil opinion of Allah, until he gives up hope of His help. For this reason some have explained that "lan yansurahu Allah" means "lan yarzuqahu" (Allah will not provide for him).

This second opinion is preferred over the first for two reasons. One: this opinion fits the one who worships Allah on the edge (of faith), for when a trial befalls him he turns back and despairs, until he thinks that Allah will not help him. Thus this statement is connected to what precedes it, and this is indicated by His saying before this verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ [al-Hajj: 14], meaning: affairs are in the hand of Allah, so no one should be discontented with the decree of Allah, nor turn back when a trial befalls him. The second reason: the pronoun in "yansurahu" according to this opinion refers to what precedes it, whereas according to the first opinion it does not refer to anything previously mentioned, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was not mentioned before in a way that the pronoun would refer to him, and the context of the speech does not clearly indicate it.

﴿Then let him look: does his plan remove what enrages him?﴾ The "kayd" (plan) here is intended to mean his strangling himself, and it is called "kayd" because he has placed it in the position of a plot, since it is the ultimate of his cunning. The meaning: if he strangles himself, let him see whether that removes what enrages him from the matter, i.e., it does not remove it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 16:

﴿And thus did We send it down﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, i.e., in this manner We sent down the entire Qur'an ﴿as clear signs, and that Allah guides whom He wills﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Anna (أن) is in the position of the predicate of the inchoative (mubtada'), and the estimate is 'the matter is that Allah...', and this is weak, because it involves an unnecessary supposition of an omitted element and cuts the speech off from the meaning preceding it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The estimate is: because Allah guides whom He wills, We sent it down thus as clear signs," so he made anna (أن) a causal clause for the sending down. This is weak, because of the separation between them by the conjunction waw (و).

The sound view, in my opinion, is that His saying ﴿and that Allah﴾ (وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ) is conjoined to "clear signs" (آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ), because it is equivalent in meaning to a verbal noun (مصدر, masdar), so the estimate is: We sent it down as clear signs and as guidance for whomever Allah wills to guide.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 17:

﴿And those who are Sabeans﴾ — mentioned in al-Baqarah [2:62]. Likewise, ﴿those who are Jews﴾. ﴿And the Magians﴾ are those who worship fire, and who say: good comes from light and evil comes from darkness. ﴿And those who associate partners [with Allah]﴾ are those who worship idols, from among the Arabs and others. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ — this sentence is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾, the verse. It is repeated with the predicate for emphasis (ta'kid). Allah's judging between them is by making clear to them that faith is the truth and all other religions are false, and by admitting those who believe into Paradise while the others enter the Fire.

It is included in this that those in the heavens among the angels, and those on the earth among the angels, and the jinn, but mankind is not included in this, because He mentioned them at the end of the verse, unless their mention at its end is in the manner of tajrid (a separate, distinct mention). The prostration meant here is not the familiar prostration, because it is not valid with regard to the sun, the moon, and what is mentioned after them. Rather, what is meant by it is submission (inqiyad). Submission is of two kinds: one is submission to the obedience of God willingly, and the other is submission to what God brings about in created beings through His actions and governance, whether they wish it or not. ﴿And many of mankind﴾: if we make prostration mean submission to the obedience of God, then "many of mankind" is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it of the things that prostrate, and His saying ﴿and many have the punishment justly due to them﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) meaning those who do not submit to obedience, and one stops at His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾. This view is the correct one. But if we make prostration mean submission to God's decree and governance, then it is not valid to distinguish between those who prostrate and those who do not, because all of them prostrate in that sense. It has been said that His saying ﴿and many of mankind﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, then ﴿and many﴾ is conjoined to it, ﴿have the punishment justly due to them﴾, so all of them prostrate on this view. But this is weak, because His saying ﴿have the punishment justly due to them﴾ apparently implies that the punishment was justly due to them only because of their abandoning prostration. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it according to this meaning, by taking the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of ﴿and many of mankind﴾ as the subject (fa'il) of a suppressed verb whose estimated form is "prostrates in the prostration of obedience", or as nominative by inception (mubtada') with a suppressed predicate whose estimated form is "rewarded". This is a far-fetched strained interpretation.

This is the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 19:

﴿These are two adversaries (hadhani khasmani)﴾ The indication (al-ishara) is to the believers and the disbelievers in general, and what is mentioned before it, namely the difference among people in their religions, indicates this. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. It is said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and 'Ubayda ibn al-Harith when they came forward on the Day of Badr against 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba. According to this, the verse is Madani up to the completion of six verses. The word khasm (adversary) applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural, and what is intended here is the plural. The indication by "these two groups" (hadhan) refers to the two groups, ﴿who dispute concerning their Lord﴾, i.e., concerning His religion and His attributes. The pronoun in "they disputed" (ikhtasamu) refers to the collective of the two groups. ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾ up to the verse: it is a judgment between the two groups, by making the Fire for the disbelievers and the Garden mentioned after this for the believers. ﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, i.e., they will be tailored to the measure of their bodies, and this is a metaphor drawn from the tailoring of garments. ﴿Boiling water (al-hamim)﴾ means hot water.

ﷻ﴿Whereby that which is in their bellies will be melted away﴾. That is, it will be melted. This is because when the scalding water (al-hamim) is poured over their heads, its heat reaches their bellies and melts what is in them. It was also said: the meaning of yusharu (is melted) is that it will be cooked.
﴿مَّقَامِعُ﴾ is the plural of مقمعة (miqma'ah), meaning a striking rod (مقرعة), ﴿مِنْ حَدِيدٍ﴾ (of iron), with which they are struck. It was also said that they are whips (السياط).
﴿From distress﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, grammatical substitution or apposition) for the genitive preceding it. ﴿And taste﴾: the implied sense (*al-taqdir*) is that it is said to them, "Taste."

﴿مِنْ أَسَاوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ﴾: The *min* here is either explanatory (*li-bayan al-jins*), indicating the kind, or partitive (*lil-tab'id*). We have explained *asawir* (bracelets) in *al-Kahf* [31].

﴿وَلُؤْلُؤاً﴾ (and pearls): This is an object of an implied verb, meaning "they will be given pearls." Alternatively, it is coordinated with the place (*mahall*) of ﴿مِنْ أَسَاوِرَ﴾, since that phrase is in the accusative as an object. When read in the genitive (*bi-l-khafd*), *lu'lu'an* is coordinated either with *asawir* or with *dhahab*.

﴿The goodly speech﴾. It was said: it is "there is no god but Allah," though the wording is more general than that. ﴿The path of the Praiseworthy﴾, meaning the path of Allah, so al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy) is a name of Allah. It is also possible that it means the praiseworthy path, and he attributed the adjective to the noun it describes, as when you say: مسجد الجامع (masjid al-jami'), "the congregational mosque."

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾: its predicate (khabar) is omitted, and it is indicated by His saying ﴿We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. It was also said that the predicate is ﴿and hinder﴾, with the waw being extra (ziyadat al-waw). This view is weak. He used the present tense, ﴿yasudduna﴾, to indicate the continuity of the action.

﴿Equal﴾ (sawa'an) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is understood. The whole clause is in the position of the second object (maf'ul thani) of ja'alna (We made). Hafs read it in the accusative, making it the second object, with ﴿the one who resides there﴾ (al-'akif) as its subject (fa'il).

﴿Al-'akif fihi wal-bad﴾ ﴿the one who resides there and the visitor﴾: al-'akif is the one who dwells in the city, and al-bad is the one who comes to it from elsewhere. The meaning is that people are equal in the Sacred Mosque; no one is singled out over another, and this is a consensus (ijma'). Abu Hanifah said that the ruling for the rest of Makkah is the same as for the Sacred Mosque in this respect: it is permissible for the visitor to lodge wherever he wishes within it, and no one owns property there. According to him, the Sacred Mosque refers to all of Makkah. Malik and others said that houses are not like the mosque in this respect, but are owned as property.

﴿With deviation through wrongdoing﴾: ilhad is deviation from what is right, and zulm (wrongdoing) here is general, covering sins from disbelief down to minor offences, because sins committed in Makkah are more grave than elsewhere. It was also said that it means making lawful what is forbidden.

The object of ﴿yurid (intends)﴾ is omitted; its estimated form is: "whoever intends anyone," or "whoever intends anything." ﴿With deviation, with wrongdoing﴾ are two synonymous circumstantial accusatives (hal, pl. ahwal, circumstantial clauses). It was also said that the object is the phrase bi-ilhad, with the ba' (with) being extra (ziyadat al-ba').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 26:

﴿And [remember] when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House﴾. The verb governing "idh" (when) is implied, its estimated form being "udhkur" (remember). And "bawwa'na" (We settled) is originally from "ba'a" (to return), meaning to return; it was then doubled to make it transitive, and it is used in the sense of "anzalna" (We caused to dwell) in the place, as in His saying: ﴿He settles the believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 121]. However, this meaning presents a difficulty here because of His saying "li-Ibrahim" (for Ibrahim), since the verb is transitive with the preposition "lam" (for), whereas it is transitive by itself, so much so that it was said: the "lam" is redundant (za'idah); and it was said: its meaning is "hayya'na" (We prepared); and it was said: "ja'alna" (We made). "Al-Bayt" (the House) here is the Ka'bah. It is related that Adam used to worship Allah in it, then it was effaced by the Flood, so Allah guided Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to its place and commanded him to build it. ﴿That you do not associate﴾: "an" (that) is explanatory (mufassirah), and the address is to Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The settling of the House was explained by the prohibition of associating partners and the command to purify, because the settling was intended only for the sake of worship, which requires that. ﴿And purify My House﴾: it is general in purifying it from disbelief, sins, impurities, and other things. ﴿And those who stand﴾: meaning those who pray.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 27:

﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾. The address is to Ibrahim (Abraham). It is also said that it is addressed to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first view is the correct one. It is narrated that when he was commanded to proclaim the pilgrimage, he climbed Mount Abu Qubays and called out: "O people, indeed Allah has commanded you to perform the pilgrimage to this House, so make pilgrimage!" Everyone who would perform the pilgrimage until the Day of Resurrection heard him, while they were in the loins of their fathers. And every thing, whether inanimate or otherwise, responded to him at that time: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am!" (labbayk Allahumma labbayk). Thus the talbiyah (the pilgrim's chant of response) continued on that basis. ﴿They will come to you on foot﴾: "rijal" is the plural of "rajil," meaning walking on their feet. ﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: "damir" is intended to mean every mount, such as a horse, a she-camel, or other things. He described it as "lean" (damir) because it does not reach the House except after becoming lean. His words ﴿and upon every lean camel﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) coordinated with another circumstantial clause, as if he had said: "on foot and riding." Some scholars have used the mention of the foot-travelers first in the verse as evidence that walking to the Hajj is better than riding. Others have used the omission of mention of the sea in this verse as evidence that the obligation of Hajj falls from one who would need to travel by sea. ﴿They will come from every deep ravine﴾ — "yati" is an attribute of every "damir," because it carries the meaning of the plural. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾: that is, a distant path.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 28:

﴿Manāfiʿa lahum﴾: that is, [gains] through trade. It was also said: the acts of Hajj and its reward; but the wording is more general than that. ﴿And mention the name of Allah﴾: meaning the invocation (tasmiyah) at the slaughter of the beasts and their sacrifice, and in the offerings (hadaya) and sacrificial animals (ḍaḥāyā). It was also said: it means remembrance (dhikr) in general. He said ﴿the name of Allah﴾ only because remembrance by the tongue is expressed through the utterance of names. ﴿On known days﴾: according to Malik, these are the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr) and the two days after it specifically, because these are the days of sacrifice in his view, and he did not permit slaughtering at night, based on His saying ﴿on days﴾. It was also said: the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, the Day of Sacrifice, and the three days after it. It was also said: the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah specifically. As for the counted days (al-ayyam al-maʿdudat), they are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice. So the Day of Sacrifice is among the known days but not among the counted days, and the two days after it are among both the known and the counted days, and the fourth day of sacrifice is among the counted days but not among the known days. ﴿So eat from them﴾: this is recommendation (nadb) or permission (ibahah), and it is recommended that one eat a smaller portion of the sacrificial animals and give away the larger portion in charity. ﴿The poor (al-baʾis)﴾: one who has been struck by hardship (al-bu's). It was also said: he is the one who begs (al-mutakaffif). It was also said: one on whom the effect of hunger is visible.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 29:

﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness (tafath)﴾ Tafath, linguistically, means filth/dirt. So the meaning is: let them remove their tafath by trimming the nails, shaving the pubic hair, and the other matters of the fitrah (natural practices) and cleanliness, after they have come out of the state of ihram (ihlal) for Hajj. It was also said: tafath refers to the rites of Hajj. It is read with a kasra and with a sukun on the lam (liyaqdi / liyaqdu), and the lam here is the lam of command, and likewise in ﴿and let them fulfill﴾ (walyuwfu) and ﴿and let them circumambulate﴾ (walyattawwafu).

﴿And let them circumambulate﴾ (walyattawwafu): the intended meaning here, according to all the exegetes, is the Tawaf al-Ifadah (the circumambulation of ifadah), which is the obligatory circumambulation, ﴿the Ancient House﴾ (bil-bayt al-ateeq), meaning the old, because it is the first House established for mankind. It was also said: al-ateeq means the noble, as in their saying "a noble horse" (faras ateeq). And it was said: it was freed (uʻtiqa) from the tyrants, meaning it was protected from them. And it was said: al-ateeq is the one that no one has ever possessed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 30:

﴿That﴾ here and in the second place is in the nominative case, on the assumption of an implied subject: "The matter is that," as a writer introduces a section of his book by saying, "This is such-and-such." Some scholars permitted a pause (waqf) after ﴿That﴾ in three places in this surah: here; at ﴿That, and whoever honours the rites of God﴾ [22:32]; and at ﴿That, and whoever associates others with God﴾ [22:31], because it is an independent clause, or because it is the predicate of an implied subject. The better view, according to our shaykh Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr, is to connect it to what follows, since what follows is not an unrelated statement. Similar examples are ﴿That, and whoever retaliates﴾ [22:60], ﴿That, so taste it﴾ [8:14] in Surat al-Anfal, and ﴿This; and indeed for the transgressors﴾ in Sad [38:55].

﴿Sacred ordinances of God﴾: the plural of ḥurma, which means whatever is not permissible to violate among the rulings of the Shari'ah (the sacred law). It may be meant here in general terms, or it may be restricted to what relates to the Hajj, since the verse is about it.

﴿It is better for him﴾: that is, honouring the sacred ordinances is better for him.

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾: that is, what He prohibited in other places, such as carrion.

﴿The abomination of idols﴾: the min here is explanatory (li-bayan al-jins), as if He said: "the abomination which is the idols." The intended meaning is the prohibition of worshipping them, or of slaughtering in their honour, as the Arabs used to do.

﴿The word of falsehood﴾: that is, lying. It was also said: it means false testimony.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 31:

﴿Then it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾ (the verse), an illustration of the polytheist as one who has brought upon himself the most severe destruction. ﴿Far away﴾ means distant.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 32:

﴿The rites of Allah﴾ It has been said: these are the offerings (hady) for the Hajj, and glorifying them means choosing animals that are fat, large, and high in price. It has also been said: they are the places of Hajj, such as ʿArafat, Mina, and Muzdalifah, and glorifying them means honouring them, showing reverence for them, and intending to visit them. It has further been said: the rites (shaʿaʾir) are the matters of the religion in general, and glorifying them means performing them and honouring them. ﴿Indeed, it is from the piety of the hearts﴾ The pronoun refers to the act implied by the statement, which is the verbal noun of "to glorify." Al-Zamakhshari said: the full sense is, "Indeed, glorifying them is one of the actions of those whose hearts are pious," so these added words have been omitted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 33:

﴿For you therein are benefits﴾. Whoever says that the symbols of God (sha'a'ir Allah) are the sacrificial animals (al-hada'a), then the benefits in them are drinking their milk, riding them for one who is compelled to do so, and the appointed term (al-ajal al-musamma) is their slaughter. And whoever says that the symbols of God are the places of Hajj, then the benefits are trade in them or reward, and the appointed term is the return to Makkah for the Tawaf al-Ifadah. ﴿Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾. Whoever says that the symbols of God are the sacrificial animals, then their place (mahill) is the place of their slaughter, which is Mina and Makkah. He singled out the House by mention because it is the most noble part of the Sacred Precinct (al-haram) and it is the intended destination of the offering (al-hady). And the "thumma" (then) according to this view is not for sequence in time, because their place is before their slaughter; rather it is for sequencing the clauses (al-jumal). And whoever says that the symbols are the places of Hajj, then their place (mahill) is taken from the release of the muhrim (ihlal al-muhrim), i.e., postpone all of that until the Tawaf at the House, meaning the Tawaf al-Ifadah, since by it the muhrim is released from his ihram. And whoever says that the symbols are the matters of the religion in general, that does not agree with his statement: "their place is at the House."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 34–36:

﴿And for every community We have appointed rites﴾: that is, for every believing community. The word mansak (mansak) is a noun of place, meaning the location of their worship. It may also be a verbal noun meaning worship. What is meant by it is the sacrifices, due to His saying: ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the cattle of grazing animals﴾, unlike what the disbelievers do of slaughtering to draw near to idols. ﴿So your God is one God﴾. There are two views on how this connects to what precedes it. First, when He mentioned the earlier nations, He addressed them with His saying: ﴿So your God is one God﴾, meaning: He is the One who prescribed the rites for you and for those before you. Second, it refers to the sacrifices, meaning: your God is one God, so do not slaughter in drawing near to other than Him. ﴿Those who are humble (al-mukhbitin)﴾: the submissive, the humble. It was said: the humble. It was also said: they were revealed concerning Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman and ʿAli, and likewise His saying after that: ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾ [al-Hajj: 37]. The wording in both is more general than that. ﴿Their hearts tremble (wajilat)﴾: were fearful. ﴿And the camels (al-budn)﴾: plural of badanah, which is what is marked from the camels. It is disputed whether a cow may be called badanah. Its position is by a verb understood. ﴿Of the rites of Allah (min shaʿaʾir Allah)﴾: its singular is shaʿirah, and min is partitive. Whoever said that the rites of Allah mentioned are restricted, or general in matters of religion, used this as evidence. ﴿In them is good for you (lakum fiha khayr)﴾: it was said the good here is the benefits mentioned before; it was said it is reward; and the correct view is generality, the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾: its meaning is: standing, having arranged their forelegs and hind legs. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state from the pronoun in the genitive, and its pattern is fawaʿil, and its singular is saffah. ﴿Then when their sides fall (wajabat junubuha)﴾: that is, they fall to the ground at their death. It is said: the wall or other things fell (wajaba) when they collapsed. ﴿The contented (al-qaniʿ)﴾: its meaning is the one who asks. It is from your saying: qana'a al-rajul (with a fatha on the nun), when he asked. It was also said: its meaning is the one who abstains from asking; on this view it is from your saying qanaʿa (with a kasra), when he was content with little. ﴿And the one who shows need (al-muʿtarr)﴾: the one who presents himself without asking. Its pattern is mufta'il. It is said: iʿtarartu bil-qawm, when I presented myself before the people. The meaning is: feed the one who asks and the one who does not ask, of those who present themselves by the tongue of their state, and feed the one who entirely abstains from asking, and the one who presents himself for giving. ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾: that is, just as We commanded you with all of this, We subjected them to you. Al-Zamakhshari said: the estimate is: like the choice you have come to know, We subjected them to you.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 37:

﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches God; rather, it is your piety that reaches Him.﴾ The meaning: you will not reach the pleasure of God through the flesh or the blood, but you reach it through taqwa (God-consciousness), that is, through sincerity toward God and intending the face of God with what you slaughter and sacrifice of offerings. This meaning is expressed with the phrase ﴿yanal﴾ (reaches) for emphasis and reinforcement, because the sense is: their flesh and their blood do not reach God, but the taqwa from you reaches Him, for that is what is required of you, and by it you obtain reward. It is said: the people of the Jahiliyyah used to smear the House with blood, so the Muslims wanted to do the same, but they were forbidden from it, and the verse was revealed. ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾ is repeated for emphasis. ﴿So that you may magnify God﴾ It is said: this means the words of the slaughterer: "Bismillah, Allahu akbar" (In the name of God, God is greatest), though the wording is more general than that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed.﴾ The disbelievers were harming the believers in Makkah, so Allah promised them that He would repel from them their evil and their harm. The object of yudafi' (defends) has been omitted so that the meaning becomes greater and more general. It has also been read as yudafi' with an alif, and as yadfa' with a sukun on the dal without an alif; both have the same meaning. The form yudafi' has been treated as if it were fa'ala, as in your saying ʿāqibat al-amr (the outcome of the matter). Al-Zamakhshari said: yudafi' means that He strongly repels on their behalf, since the form indicates intensification, and the form of mutual contest (mufa'alah) is stronger. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ Khawwan is an intensive form of khā'in (treacherous), and kafur is an intensive form of kafir (ungrateful, disbelieving). Al-Zamakhshari said: this verse is the reason (ʿillah) for what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 39:

﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought﴾. This is the first verse revealed concerning permission to fight, and it abrogated (naskh) the truce (muwada'ah) with the disbelievers. Its revelation took place at the time of the Hijrah. It is also recited as ﴿udhina﴾ with a dammah on the hamzah, in the passive form (al-bina' lima lam yusamma fa'iluh), and with a fathah, in the active form (al-bina' lil-fa'il), where the agent is Allah, exalted is He. The meaning is: He permitted them to fight, and the object of the permission is omitted because ﴿yuqatalun﴾ indicates it. ﴿Yuqatalun﴾ is also recited with a fathah and with a kasrah on the letter ta'. ﴿Because they have been wronged﴾, that is, because they were wronged.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 40:

﴿Those who were expelled from their homes﴾ means the Companions, for the disbelievers harmed them and oppressed them until they forced them to leave Makkah. Some of them migrated to the land of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), and some migrated to Madinah. The expulsion is attributed to the disbelievers because the discourse is set in the context of holding them responsible for the sin and describing them as wrongdoers. ﴿Except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah."﴾ Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), in which substitution (badal) is not permitted according to Sibawayh. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿that they say﴾ is in the place of a genitive (mahall al-jarr) as a substitution (badal) for "haqq" (right/cause). ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people...﴾ This verse reinforces the permission to fight and shows the benefit within it, as if to say: were it not for fighting and jihad, the disbelievers would have overpowered the Muslims and the religion would have perished. It was also said that the meaning is: were it not for the repelling of the oppression of oppressors by the justice of rulers; but the first interpretation is more fitting to the context of the verse. Nafi' read "difa'" with an alif, as a verbal noun of "dafa'a," while the rest read it without an alif, as a verbal noun of "dafa'a" (the form "daf'" ). ﴿Would have been demolished﴾: Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with the lighter form, while the rest read it with the doubled form (tashdid) for intensification. ﴿Monasteries (sawami')﴾ is the plural of "sawma'a," with the mim vowelled with a fatha, and it is a place of worship. It belonged to the Sabians and to the monks of the Christians. Later, in Islam, the term was applied to the place of the call to prayer (adhan). ﴿Churches (biya')﴾ is the plural of "bay'a," with the ba' vowelled with a kasra, and it refers to the churches of the Christians. ﴿Synagogues (salawat)﴾ refers to the synagogues of the Jews. It was also said that the term is shared by every community, and that what is meant by it is the places of prayer, while the mosques are for the Muslims. The meaning, then, is: were it not for Allah's repelling, the disbelievers would have overpowered the people of the earlier religions in their times, and the polytheists would have overpowered this community and demolished the places of their worship. ﴿In which the name of Allah is mentioned﴾: the pronoun refers to all the places of worship mentioned above; it was also said that it refers to the mosques specifically. ﴿And Allah will surely support whoever supports Him﴾: that is, whoever supports His religion and His friends. This is a promise that carries an exhortation to fight.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 41:

﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, they establish prayer and give zakah and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ (the verse). It is said: it means the Ummah of our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: it means the Companions. And it is said: it means the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs (al-Khulafa' al-Arba'ah), because they are the ones who were established in the land through the caliphate, and so they did what Allah described them as doing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verses 42–46:

﴿And if they deny you﴾ The subject of the verb is the Quraysh, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), as a form of consolation for him and a warning to them. ﴿Nakir﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning denial (inkar). ﴿Upon their roofs (ʿurush)﴾: ʿurush means roofs (saqf). If the prepositional phrase is connected to "khawiyah" (ruined/fallen), then the meaning is that the roofs collapsed first and then the walls fell upon them, so the walls are above them. If the prepositional phrase and what it governs stand in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), then the meaning is that they are ruined while their roofs remain standing. ﴿And an abandoned well﴾: meaning, no water is drawn from it because its people have perished. It is narrated that this well is the Rass, and that it was at (ʿAdan) for a people from the remnants of Thamud. The more apparent view is that no specific identification is intended, because of His saying: ﴿How many a town﴾, and this expression is used to denote multiplicity. ﴿And a lofty palace (qasr mashid)﴾: meaning a building constructed with gypsum (shid), which is plaster (al-jiss). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 47:

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The poor will enter Paradise before the rich by half a day." That is five hundred years. It is also said: the meaning is that one single day of the days of punishment is like a thousand years, due to the length of the punishment, since days of hardship are long even though they are in reality short. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 51:

﴿They strove against Our verses﴾ means they strove against them by finding fault with them. It derives from your saying "sa'a fi al-amr" (he strove in the matter) when he exerted himself in it, either with the aim of setting it right or of corrupting it. ﴿Mu'ajizin﴾ with the alif means contending against, because they intended to make the author of the verses (i.e., the Prophet ﷺ) incapable, while the verses demand their incapacity, so it becomes a mufa'ala (a form implying mutual action). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the shadda and without an alif, and its meaning is that they render people incapable of Islam, that is, they hold them back from it.

**﴿from a messenger or a prophet﴾** The *nabi* (prophet) is more general than the *rasul* (messenger). Every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger. The text mentions the *rasul* first to match His words ﴿We sent﴾, and mentions the *nabi* afterward to achieve generality, because if it had mentioned only the messenger, it would not include a prophet who was not a messenger. ﴿When he desired, Satan threw into his desire.﴾

The occasion of this verse was that the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) recited Surah al-Najm at al-Masjid al-Haram, in the presence of the polytheists and the Muslims. When he reached His words, ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾, Satan threw in: "Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is to be hoped for." The polytheists heard this and rejoiced and said: "Muhammad mentions our gods with what we desire."

Scholars differ over how Satan's throwing took place. It was said: Satan himself spoke those words, and people thought that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was the one who said them, because he brought his voice close to the voice of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), until the matter was confused for the polytheists. It was also said: the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) himself spoke those words by way of error and forgetfulness, because Satan cast them and whispered into his heart, until that phrase came out of his tongue without intention. The second view is more famous among the exegetes and the transmitters of this story, while the first view is more preferable, because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is protected in conveying the message. So the meaning of the verse is that every prophet and every messenger has experienced something similar of Satan's casting.

Scholars also differed over the meaning of *tamanna* (desire) and *umniyya* (desire) in this verse. It was said: *tamanna* here means *tala* (recited), and *umniyya* means recitation. That is, when he recited the Book, Satan cast something from himself into his recitation. It was also said: it derives from *tamanni* in the sense of loving a thing, and this meaning is more common in usage. That is, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) desired to draw near to his people and win them over, and Satan cast that into this desire so as to please them.

﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan throws⁠﴾: that is, He nullifies it, as you say: "The sun *naskh*ed (abolished) the shade," meaning the *naskh* (abrogation) here is removal and cancellation.

Qur'anic quotations: "Those who were killed or died..." (verse 58), "a goodly provision" (verse 58), "an entrance" (verse 59).

**Translation:**

﴿Those who were killed or died﴾. It is related that some people said: "O Messenger of God, we know what God has bestowed of good things upon those who were killed; what then is for those who died with you?" So the verse was revealed, informing that God provides for both those who were killed and those who died (in His cause), "and surely God is the best of providers". This does not necessitate equality between them, because the preference of the martyrs is established. ﴿A goodly provision﴾ may be understood to mean the provision in Paradise after the Day of Resurrection, or the provision of the martyrs in the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection). The first is more preferred, because it encompasses both the martyrs and the dead. ﴿An entrance﴾ means Paradise.

﴿Dhalika﴾ (That is so): its sense here is "The matter is thus," as a writer says "this" and "such-and-such was the case" when he wishes to move on to another topic.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verses 62–67:

﴿That is because Allah, He is the Truth﴾: meaning, that attribute by which Allah has described Himself is because He is the Truth.

﴿Then the earth becomes green﴾: here "tusbihu" (becomes) means "tasir" (becomes). Some understood that it refers to the morning after a night of rain, and so said: the earth becomes green only in Makkah and in hot lands. But in the sense of "becomes," it is general for every land. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction (ʿatf) and is not a response (jawab). Had it been a response to His saying ﴿Do you not see﴾, the verb would have been in the subjunctive, and the meaning would have been the negation of its greenness, which contradicts the intended meaning. He said ﴿tusbihu﴾ in the present form (al-mudari'ah) to indicate that it remains so for a period of time.

﴿He has subjected to you whatever is in the earth﴾: meaning the beasts, the fruits, the minerals, and other things.

﴿Lest it fall﴾: it is in the position of an object (maf'ul) with the implied preposition "an" (from), i.e., "from falling." Al-Zamakhshari said: "for fear that it fall," so it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

﴿Except by His permission﴾: it may mean the Day of Resurrection, so that the folding of the sky is like its falling; or it may mean "by His permission," that is, if He wills, whenever He wills.

﴿He gave you life﴾: that is, He brought you into existence after non-existence. He expressed this by life, because before that a human being was dust, so he was inanimate matter without a soul, and then He gave him life by breathing the soul into him.

﴿Then He causes you to die﴾: meaning the well-known death.

﴿Then He will give you life﴾: meaning the resurrection.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful﴾: that is, deniers of the blessing.

﴿A rite﴾ (mansakan): it is a verbal noun (ism masdar) for His saying ﴿they perform it﴾ (nasikuhu). Had it been a noun of place, He would have said "nasikun fihi" (they perform in it).

﴿So let them not dispute with you﴾: the subject pronoun refers to the disbelievers. The meaning: it is not fitting to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, because the truth has become manifest such that dispute about it has no room. The verb came in the form of a prohibition while the intended meaning is other than prohibition. It was also said: the meaning is "do not dispute with them, so they will dispute with you," the first being omitted because the second indicates it. It may also be a prohibition to them from disputing, according to the apparent wording.

﴿In the matter﴾: that is, in the religion, the sharia, or in the slaughtering.

﴿And invite to your Lord﴾: that is, invite people to worship your Lord.

﴿Then the earth becomes green﴾: here "tusbihu" (becomes) means "tasir" (becomes). Some understood that it refers to the morning after a night of rain, and so said: the earth becomes green only in Makkah and in hot lands. But in the sense of "becomes," it is general for every land. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction (ʿatf) and is not a response (jawab). Had it been a response to His saying ﴿Do you not see﴾, the verb would have been in the subjunctive, and the meaning would have been the negation of its greenness, which contradicts the intended meaning. He said ﴿tusbihu﴾ in the present form (al-mudari'ah) to indicate that it remains so for a period of time.

﴿He has subjected to you whatever is in the earth﴾: meaning the beasts, the fruits, the minerals, and other things.

﴿Lest it fall﴾: it is in the position of an object (maf'ul) with the implied preposition "an" (from), i.e., "from falling." Al-Zamakhshari said: "for fear that it fall," so it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi).

﴿Except by His permission﴾: it may mean the Day of Resurrection, so that the folding of the sky is like its falling; or it may mean "by His permission," that is, if He wills, whenever He wills.

﴿He gave you life﴾: that is, He brought you into existence after non-existence. He expressed this by life, because before that a human being was dust, so he was inanimate matter without a soul, and then He gave him life by breathing the soul into him.

﴿Then He causes you to die﴾: meaning the well-known death.

﴿Then He will give you life﴾: meaning the resurrection.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful﴾: that is, deniers of the blessing.

﴿A rite﴾ (mansakan): it is a verbal noun (ism masdar) for His saying ﴿they perform it﴾ (nasikuhu). Had it been a noun of place, He would have said "nasikun fihi" (they perform in it).

﴿So let them not dispute with you﴾: the subject pronoun refers to the disbelievers. The meaning: it is not fitting to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, because the truth has become manifest such that dispute about it has no room. The verb came in the form of a prohibition while the intended meaning is other than prohibition. It was also said: the meaning is "do not dispute with them, so they will dispute with you," the first being omitted because the second indicates it. It may also be a prohibition to them from disputing, according to the apparent wording.

﴿In the matter﴾: that is, in the religion, the sharia, or in the slaughtering.

﴿And invite to your Lord﴾: that is, invite people to worship your Lord.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 22, verse 77:

﴿Bow down and prostrate yourselves﴾. In this verse there is a prostration (sajda) according to al-Shafi'i and others, on account of the authentic hadith transmitted on this matter, in contrast to the Malikis. ﴿And worship your Lord﴾: a general command to worship, after which comes the prayer, which was expressed by bowing and prostration. He mentioned it first only because it is the most important of the acts of worship. ﴿And do good﴾: it has been said that what is meant is maintaining the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim). Ibn 'Atiyya said: it refers to what is recommended (nadb), apart from the obligatory duties. But the wording is more general than all of that.

[Striving in Allah's cause] may mean striving against the disbelievers, or striving against the self (nafs), Satan, or desire (hawa), or it may be general in all of that. ﴿And strive in Allah's cause with the striving due to Him.﴾ It has been said that this is abrogated (mansukh), like the abrogation (naskh) of ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ by His words ﴿so fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [Al-Anfal: 60; At-Taghabun: 16]. But this is open to question. He attributed the striving to Allah only to show its excellence and its special connection to Allah. ﴿He has chosen you﴾, that is, He selected you from among the nations. ﴿Without hardship﴾, that is, without difficulty; the root meaning of ḥaraj is narrowness. ﴿The religion (millah) of your father Abraham﴾. The word millah is in the accusative by an implied verb, whose sense is: "I mean by the religion the millah of Abraham," or "adhere to the millah of Abraham." Al-Farra' said it is in the accusative by omitting the kaf (like), as if he said "like the millah." Al-Zamakhshari said it is in the accusative by what precedes in meaning: as if he said, "He widened [the religion] for you with the widening of the millah of your father Abraham," then the genitive was dropped. If it is asked: Abraham was not the father of all Muslims, the answer is that he was the father of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was the father of his community, because the Messenger's community is in the position of his children. For this reason it was recited, "﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾" [Al-Ahzab: 6], and "he is their father." Also, Quraysh and most of the Arabs are descendants of Abraham, and they are the majority of the nation, so he singled them out over others. ﴿He named you﴾: the pronoun refers to Allah, Exalted. The meaning of ﴿before﴾ is: in the earlier scriptures. ﴿And in this﴾, that is, in the Qur'an. It has been said that the pronoun refers to Abraham, and the reference is to his words: ﴿and from our offspring a Muslim nation for You﴾. The meaning of "before" according to this view is: before your existence. Here the statement is complete according to this view, and his words ﴿and in this﴾ begin a new sentence: that is, "and in this message." The first view is more preponderant and less forced, and it is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Allah named you Muslims." ﴿A witness over you﴾: the meaning of this testimony has already been explained in Al-Baqarah. ﴿So establish the prayer﴾: it is apparent that this means the obligatory prayer, because it is paired with zakat (obligatory charity). ﴿He is your Protector (mawla)﴾: its meaning here is: your guardian and helper, as indicated by what follows it.
